1: Nine months earlier, she had been diagnosed with idiopathic pulmonary hypertension after a 3-year history of progressive dyspnea (now NYHA class IV) and orthopnea, without cough or sputum, accompanied by low-grade fever and night sweats.

Echocardiography at that time showed a pulmonary arterial systolic pressure (PASP) of 80 mm Hg, a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60%, mild mitral regurgitation, and moderate to severe tricuspid regurgitation.
2: A 58-year-old woman presented to the rheumatology clinic with a 2-month history of fatigue, weakness, polyarthritis, and joint swelling.

On examination, there was effusion of the right second, third, and fourth metacarpophalangeal joints; right second and third proximal interphalangeal joints; left second, third, and fourth metacarpophalangeal joints; and left fourth and fifth proximal interphalangeal joints.
Tests for anti–Scl-70, hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C virus, and rheumatoid arthritis were negative.
4: Nine months earlier, she had been diagnosed with idiopathic pulmonary hypertension after a 3-year history of progressive dyspnea (now NYHA class IV) and orthopnea, without cough or sputum, accompanied by low-grade fever and night sweats.

Echocardiography at that time showed a pulmonary arterial systolic pressure (PASP) of 80 mm Hg, a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60%, mild mitral regurgitation, and moderate to severe tricuspid regurgitation.
Raynaud’s phenomenon was elicited by cold‐water immersion of the hands.
Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 45 mm/h, an antinuclear antibody titer of 1:320, and an anti-centromere antibody level of 94.8 AU/ml.
Tests for anti–Scl-70, hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C virus, and rheumatoid arthritis were negative.
